answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — a Victorian commonplace
answer.authorDates: 1824–1905 · Scottish novelist, poet & minister whose books deeply shaped C.S. Lewis
answer.sourceLine: C.S. Lewis never wrote this — it appears in none of his works, and the C.S. Lewis Foundation lists it as its single most common misattribution. The thought is a 19th-century pulpit commonplace: documented as early as an 1881 Church Congress paper by Rev. Dr. R. Thornton and credited (secondhand and unsourced) to George MacDonald in an 1892 Quaker periodical, while the exact modern three-part wording matches Walter M. Miller Jr.’s 1959 novel A Canticle for Leibowitz.

source.excerpt: They ought to be taught that they have bodies, and that their bodies die; while they themselves live on … that we talk as if we possessed souls, instead of being souls.
trail: The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists this as a misattribution, calling it a paraphrase of George MacDonald’s Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood.
Mere Orthodoxy traces the phrasing through an 1892 Quaker attribution to MacDonald and a string of pre-Lewis sources (1895, 1901, 1905, 1929).
First Things pushes the earliest documented use back to Rev. Dr. R. Thornton’s 1881 Church Congress paper, later reprinted in Spiritualist periodicals.
Fauxtations quotes Wikiquote: “Commonly attributed to Mere Christianity, where it is not found.”
source.excerptNote: George MacDonald’s actual words in Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood (1867) — the sentiment, but not the neat three-part slogan later pinned on Lewis. The crisp modern phrasing is closest to Walter M. Miller Jr.: “You don’t have a soul, Doctor. You are a soul. You have a body, temporarily.”

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording cannot be tied to any single pre-Lewis work. The nearest named source, George MacDonald’s Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood (1867), is public domain but does not contain this three-part phrasing; the closest exact match, Walter M. Miller Jr.’s A Canticle for Leibowitz (1959), is in-copyright but uses a variant. With no sourceable origin for the wording as circulated, no rights status can honestly be asserted.

author.name: George MacDonald
author.kicker: Not the man it’s credited to
author.heading: About the nearest real source
author.bio: George MacDonald was a Scottish author and minister whose fantasy and fiction — Phantastes, Lilith, the Curdie books — profoundly influenced C.S. Lewis, who called him his “master.” In Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood (1867) he argued that we should speak of being souls rather than merely having them. That affinity is exactly why a slogan he never quite wrote drifted onto Lewis’s name a century later.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on C.S. Lewis
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared “C.S. Lewis” lines — and one he never wrote. Here is the tangle behind it.

items.why: The line appears in none of Lewis’s books, essays or letters; it is routinely credited to Mere Christianity, where it is simply not found. The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists it as its single most common misattribution.

MacDonald is the nearest real source — an 1892 Quaker periodical credits a version to him — and his 1867 Annals voices the idea (“we talk as if we possessed souls, instead of being souls”), but not this tidy three-part slogan. Lewis’s devotion to MacDonald is likely why the line migrated to his name.
His 1959 novel A Canticle for Leibowitz carries the closest exact wording, but Miller did not originate the sentiment, which predates him by decades.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s a Victorian pulpit commonplace, documented from 1881 onward and never traceable to C.S. Lewis at all.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Lewis
lead: The quote feels like Lewis because it is brisk, aphoristic, and Christian-Platonist — and because Lewis openly revered George MacDonald, to whom the idea is most often traced. Attach a memorable slogan to a beloved name and it travels; the name gives the words authority the words alone can’t earn.

In reality the sentiment was a shared 19th-century pulpit trope, surfacing in Church Congress papers, Quaker periodicals, YMCA manuals and novels long before Lewis put pen to paper — and, ironically, Lewis himself rejected any neat body-soul dualism, writing elsewhere of the two in “organic unity.”
context.pull: Lewis never wrote it — but he loved the man it’s really borrowed from.
